papers.title: Auditing Safety Preference Supervision with Recorded Derivations
papers.abstract: Preference labels align model training, but the judgments behind them are difficult to inspect or verify. In this paper, we examine how preference construction can be checked when intermediate decisions are recorded, and which of them remain uncertain. We present Symbolic Preference Labeling, a method in which a pretrained language model classifies predefined attributes of prompts and responses. Explicit rules assign response verdicts, and a fixed verdict ranking determines the preference label. Each preference label has a recorded derivation: the response verdicts and preference label can be recomputed from the stored attribute assignments, rules, and verdict ranking without rerunning the language model. On 200 prompts annotated by human raters, the language model produces valid structured outputs for 192 prompts. All eight parsing failures occur in the subset of self-harm prompts marked as harmful. Using 465 preference pairs, we train one policy model with direct preference optimization across five training seeds. Mean measured benign refusal is 40.82 percent on 1,319 benign prompts that resemble unsafe ones, and mean measured toxic refusal is 84.98 percent on 655 toxic prompts. This study distinguishes the reproducibility of preference labels from attribute correctness. The recorded derivations make preference construction open to inspection, while attribute correctness and semantic safety require separate validation.

papers.title: OptScientist: Automated Discovery of Optimization Laws
papers.abstract: Many scientific phenomena are best understood as outcomes of underlying optimization problems, yet automated scientific discovery has largely focused on recovering equations that describe observed input-output patterns. We introduce OptScientist, a novel automated framework for discovering compact symbolic optimization laws directly from data. OptScientist comprises (i) a model that infers symbolic optimization problems by first learning to represent data as an optimization problem and then extracting its symbolic form, and (ii) an LLM agentic system embedding the model in a discovery process that integrates theoretical priors from scientific literature, discovers candidate laws, abstracts their underlying mechanisms, and suggests new data to collect. We first evaluate OptScientist on OptFeynman, a novel benchmark of 99 physics-derived optimization problems, where OptScientist recovers ground-truth laws for over 80% of the problems and remains robust to noisy contextual information, while substantially outperforming machine-learning, symbolic, and LLM-based model-discovery baselines. On human risky choice and central-bank monetary policy, OptScientist discovers compact symbolic optimization laws that achieve held-out predictive performance competitive with leading baselines, while using few parameters and substantially fewer tokens than LLM baselines. Overall, OptScientist extends automated scientific discovery to uncovering optimization laws that generate observed phenomena, enabling automated theory building across the physical, biological, behavioral, and social sciences.

papers.title: A 55-Addition Rank-23 Scheme for $3\times3$ Matrix Multiplication via Exact Two-Sided Minimization
papers.abstract: We give a scheme that multiplies two $3\times3$ matrices with 23 multiplications and 55 additions over any ring, one addition below the previous record of 56 (Sun, 2026) and the first below 56 for exact non-commutative $3\times3$ multiplication without a change of basis. The scheme forms 13 signed combinations of the entries of A and 14 of B, takes 23 products, and recombines them with 28 further additions; its correctness is machine-checked in Lean 4. The previous records, from 60 down to 56, were obtained by greedy common-subexpression elimination, which only bounds each side of a scheme from above. We minimize both input sides exactly by chain covering, and the output side exactly through the transposition principle: the 9-by-23 output map costs its transpose plus 14, and the transpose is a 9-input map that the input-side minimizer solves exactly. Applied to Perminov's cn122 scheme (class i19w225c4efh, published at 58 additions) this gives 55 = 13 + 14 + 28, where greedy elimination reaches only 29 on the output side. The same method shows that Sun's representative is output-optimal at 56, and an exact orbit-wide computation over the Heule-Kauers-Seidl database shows that the record class is the only database class attaining 55.

papers.title: Racer: Hunting GPU Kernel Bugs with Symbolic Equivalence Checking
papers.abstract: GPU kernels are critical to the performance of today's AI services, yet the same operators are rewritten repeatedly: for each GPU generation, numeric format, serving regime, and kernel language. Every rewrite must preserve the function computed by the implementation it replaces. Today, this obligation depends almost entirely on differential testing: run the new kernel and a trusted reference on randomly sampled tensors, then compare their outputs within a tolerance. This approach has blind spots that additional test cases cannot eliminate. For example, a logical bug may produce an error smaller than the tolerance required to accommodate a correct optimized kernel. We propose symbolic equivalence checking, which executes a kernel and its reference on symbolic inputs, turning each output cell into an exact algebraic expression, and then checks whether the paired expressions agree for all inputs. Because these expressions are exact, symbolic equivalence checking distinguishes floating-point error from logical bugs, while a single check covers the entire input space. We implement Racer, a PTX-level symbolic equivalence checking engine, with three techniques that make this approach practical for production kernels: (1) Shape Reduction to control checking cost, (2) a lockstep CTA scheduler to handle concurrency, and (3) idiom templates with exact numeric refutation for otherwise inconclusive results. Across 2,408 production kernels from 41 collection targets, Racer found 82 real bugs in 23 libraries, including 76 previously unknown bugs and 41 confirmed so far.

papers.title: The Indefinite Summation Problem for the Laurent Ring
papers.abstract: This article solves the Indefinite Summation Problem (ISP) for the difference ring $(A, \alpha)$, where $A$ is the Laurent ring of shift operators on the lattice $\Z^n$, and $\alpha$ is any ring automorphism of $A$ of finite order. The space of summable elements in $(A, \alpha)$ is infinite dimensional, and it is possible to write down an explicit basis for it. The solution translates to a finite procedure involving a matrix multiplication, where the size of the matrix can be estimated. It follows that the arithmetic complexity of the solution can also be determined. These results extend to a solution of the ISP for the ring of functions on $\Z^n$, on which $\alpha$ acts by duality. The article also points out that the solution to the ISP amounts to calculating the group cohomologies $H^i([\alpha], A), i = 0, 1$, where $[\alpha]$ is the cyclic group generated by $\alpha$.
